rationale: obs[S1]: AllMusic styles the album Fusion, Jazz-Rock and Post-Bop and records May 26 & May 28, 1969; the AllMusic review calls it 'one of the first and most influential albums in late-'60s fusion' that 'shattered the boundaries between jazz and rock.' obs[S2]: Wikipedia documents the trio personnel (John McLaughlin, Larry Young, Tony Williams), track listing, producers Monte Kay/Jack Lewis and engineer Gene Radice. obs[S3]: MusicBrainz release group confirms the original 1969 Polydor release. inf: The record is a direct pre-fusion bridge — it brings three Miles Davis sidemen (Williams from the 1960s quintet, McLaughlin and Young from the Bitches Brew orbit) into a rock-volume, organ-guitar-drums trio months before Bitches Brew appeared, making the later electric diaspora audible. unk: The trio is constant across tracks, but per-take overdubs or edits are not documented in the consulted sources.
bridge_case: Connects the Miles Davis acoustic and early-electric bands to the jazz-rock trio format McLaughlin and Cobham would soon push with Mahavishnu Orchestra; it is the sound of the sideman diaspora leaving the quintet behind.
scope_flag: Fusion gate — rock rhythm, organ/guitar amplification, and the jazz-rock trio language are the organizing idea; the case-against is that its raw, double-LP sprawl can sound more like a rock experiment than a jazz lineage statement.

scope_check.boundary_note: The 1969 date is in range, but this is a fusion-gate boundary case: amplified guitar and Hammond organ, rock-volume attack, and jazz-rock rhythm are central to its language, so the bridge test—not mere admissibility—must decide it.

ballot.case_for: Emergency! is an exceptionally direct bridge from the late-1960s Miles Davis/post-bop world into electric jazz: Tony Williams, John McLaughlin, and Larry Young turn the harmonic and rhythmic freedom of that lineage into a power-trio language months before Bitches Brew. AllMusic calls it one of the first and most influential late-1960s fusion albums and identifies it as Fusion, Jazz-Rock, and Post-Bop (S1); the constant trio documented in the dossier gives the date unusual session gravity. Its influence is audible in the electric diaspora that followed, especially McLaughlin's Mahavishnu work and the broader vocabulary of 1970s fusion.
ballot.case_against: The anti-drift warning applies at full force: this raw, distorted double album often makes rock volume, guitar-organ texture, and aggressive backbeat the organizing experience rather than extending an identifiable post-bop or modal ensemble conversation. Its abrasive, sometimes muddy sound and Williams's idiosyncratic vocals can make it a poor cold-entry discovery record, so historical importance alone may not outweigh its distance from the canon's center. The dossier establishes basic discographical facts well but offers limited independent critical-consensus evidence beyond AllMusic (S1).
ballot.recommendation: The council proposes that John treat Emergency! as a strong but genuine fusion-boundary ruling: retain it only if he wants the canon to document the Miles-era electric break at its most raw and rock-forward.
